strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing T2I benchmarks use short prompts (12–84 tokens) while DETAILMASTER provides 4,116 prompts averaging ~285 tokens with four well-motivated evaluation dimensions (character attributes, locations, scene attributes, entity relationships) that specifically target structural comprehension and detail-overload failures.

Data construction is unusually careful for an LLM-driven pipeline: multi-stage validation (MLLM + open-set detector voting, BLIP scoring, LLM attribute verification), a non-trivial spatial partitioning scheme validated against the conventional 3x3 grid (Table 4), and human expert evaluation on 400 samples across fine-grained checks (Tables 5–8) with mostly near-100% scores.

Extensive and credible robustness analysis: re-running the full evaluation with an alternative MLLM (InternVL3-9B, Table 9, Kendall's tau 0.87–1.0), a randomness/seed analysis (Table 10, delta < 0.5%), a mini-benchmark preserving rankings (Table 12), and ablations of auxiliary techniques (Appendix H.3).

Evaluation of 12 models including SOTA proprietary systems (GPT Image-1, Gemini 2.0 Flash) and five long-prompt-optimized methods yields useful, actionable insights: performance plateaus near ~50% even for SOTA models on compositional dimensions; long-prompt training matters more than context-window expansion; backbone architecture constrains optimized models.
Honest limitations section (Appendix O), full open-sourcing of data, curation code (as Data-Juicer recipes), and evaluation tools, plus a resource-efficient mini-benchmark to encourage adoption.
weaknesses: The MLLM-based evaluator itself is never validated against human judgments of generated images. The human study (Section 5.2, Appendix G) validates annotations against source images and prompts, but there is no reported human agreement rate for the Qwen2.5-VL yes/no verdicts on generated images — the central measurement instrument. The cross-MLLM comparison (Appendix I) shows consistent rankings but both evaluators could share systematic errors.

Circularity risk: attributes are extracted, prompts are expanded, and accuracy is judged largely by the same Qwen model family. The authors' counterarguments (grounding via detectors, distinct text encoders in evaluated models) are plausible but not fully conclusive, and the finding that alternative evaluators systematically 'inflates' scores hints at judge-specific noise in absolute accuracy numbers.

The negative correlation between prompt length and accuracy (Section 4.3, Figure 3) is presented as a core finding but is confounded: longer prompts in this dataset also contain more attributes per character, so 'detail load' and 'length' are not disentangled. A controlled analysis (same number of attributes, varying linguistic length, or vice versa) is missing.

Prompts are LLM-expanded enumerations of detected attributes on top of real captions, which may be stylistically unnatural (repetitive attribute listing, as visible in the case studies), limiting ecological validity for the real-world long-prompt scenarios the paper motivates; the benchmark also inherits ~90% (not 100%) attribute-image alignment, i.e., some hallucinated attributes enter prompts.

Accuracy metrics exclude image quality, coherence, and aesthetics entirely; a model could satisfy many attributes with a broken image. The compatibility demonstration (Appendix K) helps but the headline numbers in Table 2 should be interpreted with this caveat, which the main text underplays.

Generation protocol details are underspecified in the main text (e.g., number of images/seeds per prompt, whether stochasticity of the generators was controlled), which matters for a benchmark whose conclusions rest on small score gaps between adjacent models (e.g., FLUX vs. Gemini).

Minor presentation issues: 'Enitity', 'Fliter', and 'inaccurately' typos, duplicated references (Wu et al. 2023b/2023c; Achiam 2023a/2023b), and Table 12/10 labeling inconsistencies ('Spatial Attributes' vs 'Entity Relationships') reduce polish.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing T2I benchmarks (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Bench, DrawBench) use short prompts, while DensePrompts and DPG-Bench are limited to ~100 tokens. DETAILMASTER's 4,116 prompts averaging 284.89 tokens with structured annotations across four dimensions (character attributes, locations, scene attributes, entity relationships) is a substantial and reusable resource.

Unusually thorough robustness analysis for a benchmark paper: cross-evaluator re-runs with InternVL3-9B reporting Kendall's Tau correlations of 0.879-1.000 (Appendix I), random-seed/temperature variance analysis showing <0.5% variation (Appendix J), ablations of auxiliary grounding techniques (Appendix H.3), and a mini-benchmark preserving ranking trends (Appendix L).

Honest treatment of the Qwen-family circularity concern (single MLLM family used for both construction and evaluation), with a reasoned argument and empirical evidence that rankings are preserved under a different evaluator.

Human expert evaluation of 400 samples across multiple fine-grained criteria (Tables 5-8) quantifying hallucination rates (e.g., 88.58% entity-relationship image alignment) rather than claiming perfect data quality.

Insightful empirical findings with practical value: the difficulty hierarchy (character locations hardest, scene attributes easiest), the observation that long-prompt training matters more than expanded context windows, and the negative correlation between prompt length and adherence across 10 models.
Comprehensive evaluation of 12 models including proprietary SOTA systems, with detailed configurations and reproducibility information (Appendices C-E, released code and data via Data-Juicer).
weaknesses: Critical metric validation gap: the benchmark's core claim rests on MLLM yes/no judgments, yet human evaluation is only performed on data quality (source images/annotations), never on whether the evaluation pipeline's judgments agree with human assessments of GENERATED images. MLLM evaluators are known to be unreliable on synthetic images (hallucinated attributes, sycophancy), and the 91-95% 'accuracy' of the pipeline on source images does not establish validity on generations. For a paper whose sole contribution is measurement, this is a significant evidential hole.

The 'first comprehensive benchmark' framing is overstated given the paper's own related work (DensePrompts, DPG-Bench); the novelty is primarily scale (longer prompts, more annotations) rather than methodology, and the construction pipeline (existing detailed captions + LLM-based attribute extraction and expansion) is a fairly standard LLM-data-engineering recipe.

Circularity concerns persist despite mitigation: Qwen models both generate the attributes that define 'ground truth' and judge whether generations satisfy them. Errors correlated between construction and evaluation (e.g., Qwen-specific attribute phrasings, hallucinated attributes that still reach prompts at ~91-89% image alignment for persons/relationships) could systematically bias absolute numbers, even if relative rankings survive the InternVL cross-check.

Prompt quality is questionable: the case studies show highly repetitive, unnaturally templated prompts (attribute lists re-stated in near-identical form), which may not reflect 'real-world long-prompt complexity' as claimed and could interact with model training-data priors in ways the paper does not analyze.

Conclusions about long-prompt optimized models are confounded: all five optimized methods run on SD1.5/SD-XL backbones from 2022, so the finding that 'backbone architectures constrain performance' partly reflects the obsolescence of available checkpoints rather than a controlled comparison, and the attribution of gains to 'long-prompt training' vs. 'token capacity' is inferred from heterogeneous systems without controlled experiments.

The negative correlation analysis (Figure 3) is purely descriptive across five coarse length bins with no statistical testing, and prompt length is confounded with number of required attributes/relationships, so 'length causes degradation' is not cleanly established versus 'more required details cause degradation.'
Only two annotators on 400 sampled instances for human evaluation; inter-annotator agreement is not reported, and no compensation/protocol details are given.

Writing has rough edges that undermine polish: duplicated references (Achiam 2023a/b, Wu 2023b/c), inconsistent terminology (e.g., 'Spatial Attributes' vs 'Entity Relationships' in Tables 10/12), and grammatical issues throughout.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly motivated gap: existing T2I benchmarks (T2I-CompBench, HRS-Comp, DPG-Bench, DensePrompts) use short prompts, while practical applications need long, detail-rich prompts; the 284.89-token average is a substantial step beyond prior ~100-token benchmarks.

Large-scale systematic evaluation of 12 models (7 general-purpose including GPT Image-1 and Gemini 2.0 Flash, 5 long-prompt-optimized) across four well-defined dimensions yields actionable insights, e.g., that long-prompt training and iterative decomposition matter more than expanded context windows, and that performance plateaus around 50% even for SOTA systems.

Unusually thorough robustness validation for a benchmark paper: human expert evaluation on 400 samples across fine-grained sub-criteria (Appendix G), cross-evaluator replication with InternVL3-9B with high Kendall's Tau correlations (Appendix I), randomness/seed analysis (Appendix J), and ablations of auxiliary pipeline techniques (Appendix H).

Comparative validation of the spatial partitioning scheme against the conventional 3x3 grid (Table 4: null labels reduced from 66.19% to 32.68% at comparable matching accuracy), and a resource-efficient mini-benchmark that preserves ranking trends (Appendix L).

Comprehensive reproducibility support: model configurations, GPU-hours, LLM prompt designs, evaluation protocol details, limitations section (Appendix O), and case studies; data, curation code, and evaluation tools are open-sourced.
weaknesses: Circularity risk in data construction and evaluation: both the benchmark's ground-truth attributes and the automatic evaluator rely on the same Qwen model family, and prompts are LLM-expanded from source captions. The mitigation arguments (auxiliary detectors, human spot-checks, InternVL re-evaluation) are reasonable but the cross-evaluator check only verifies rank correlation, not absolute accuracy correctness; an MLLM-agnostic or human-verified gold subset for full evaluation would substantially strengthen the claims.

The evaluation protocol appears to score a single generated image per prompt, with no accounting for generation stochasticity or sampling budget (Appendix J analyzes only evaluator randomness, not T2I output variance). Diffusion models have high per-prompt variance, so single-sample accuracy numbers may be noisy and could disadvantage deterministic pipelines; this should be discussed or addressed.

Metric design concerns: 'Character Attributes' treats each attribute as an independent binary judgment, so a model generating 20 of 30 attributes scores the same as one generating 0 attributes for 3 of 4 characters in a differently distributed prompt; attribute omission versus misalignment is conflated in the headline metric (partially disentangled only in Table 3). Also, prompts derived from real photographs encode positions/attributes that conflict with generative priors (acknowledged in Appendix M), which may inflate apparent failure rates in ways that do not reflect compositional capability alone.

Scene Attributes are near-saturated (>90-95% for modern models, 0.2-2.7% hard-sample rates), giving that dimension little discriminative power; meanwhile token length is measured with CLIP's tokenizer even for T5-based models, making the 'prompt length vs. adherence' analysis in Section 4.3 model-inconsistent.

The mechanistic claims in the abstract and conclusion ('encoders flatten complex grammatical structures', 'diffusion models suffer from attribute leakage') are presented as findings but are hypotheses without direct causal evidence; the paper appropriately flags this as an open question, but the abstract overstates it.

The 'first comprehensive benchmark' framing is overstated given DensePrompts and DPG-Bench; the differentiation (token length, attribute density) is real but the related-work positioning could be more measured. Human evaluation is small (400 samples, 2 annotators, no inter-annotator agreement reported).

Cross-model comparability issues: 512x512 for SD1.5-based models versus 1024x1024 for others, different guidance scales and step counts, and proprietary APIs with uncontrolled server-side defaults all introduce confounds when ranking models on an adherence benchmark.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing T2I benchmarks rely on short, synthetic, or coarse-grained prompts, while real professional workflows use long, constraint-dense instructions. The comparison against prior long-prompt benchmarks (Table 1) is convincing in terms of prompt length (avg. 284.89 tokens), annotation density, and grounding in real image-caption pairs (DOCCI, Localized Narratives) rather than purely LLM-synthesized prompts.

The data construction pipeline is carefully engineered with multiple grounding mechanisms (dual bounding-box proposals from an MLLM and YOLOE-11L reconciled via IoU/BLIP scoring, per-attribute verification, prompt-annotation synchronization checks), and the human evaluation (Section 5.2, Appendix G) provides concrete quality evidence, including honest reporting of weaker metrics (e.g., Entity Relationship-Image Alignment at 88.58%) with a reasonable argument that prompt-conditional evaluation is unaffected.

The evaluation is extensive: 19 models across five paradigms, including proprietary SOTA models and newly released ones (Nano Banana 2), with meaningful findings such as the difficulty hierarchy (Character Locations hardest) and the negative correlation between prompt length and adherence.

The controlled 2x2 ablation (token limit vs. long-prompt training, Table 3) is the most scientifically interesting component: it disentangles context-window expansion from long-prompt training and shows training data matters more, corroborated by cross-evaluation on short prompts (Appendix U) showing no degradation.

Robustness of the LLM-based evaluation is addressed unusually thoroughly for a benchmark paper: alternative evaluator (InternVL3-9B) with Kendall's Tau correlations, a smaller evaluator for resource-constrained users, randomness/seed analysis, and an explicit experiment refuting self-enhancement bias for the family-matched Qwen-Image case (Appendix J, K, L). Computational costs and configurations are documented (Appendix C, D).
weaknesses: Despite the mitigations, the benchmark's data construction and primary evaluation both hinge on a single MLLM family (Qwen2.5-VL), and absolute scores shift substantially across evaluators (e.g., FLUX.1-dev Character Locations rises from 41.57 to 67.13 with InternVL3-9B). Rank preservation is shown, but per-model absolute accuracy interpretation remains evaluator-dependent, and the yes/no binary judgments of a 7B MLLM on fine-grained attributes introduce nontrivial noise that no human-in-the-loop validation of the evaluation pipeline itself (as opposed to the dataset) fully resolves.

Annotation quality, while high, is not perfect: roughly 8-11% of person attributes and 11.4% of entity relationships do not align with source images (hallucinated attributes). The authors argue prompts are the sole supervision, which is logically consistent, but it also means the benchmark partially evaluates whether models can render MLLM-invented (potentially physically implausible) details, conflating prompt-following with prompt realism.

The length-adherence analysis (Section 4.3, Figure 3) uses raw token count as the variable, but token count is confounded with constraint density (more tokens usually means more attributes to satisfy). The paper's own framing ('high constraint density' vs. length) acknowledges this distinction, yet the correlation analysis does not disentangle number of constraints from token length, weakening the causal interpretation of the degradation finding.

Methodological originality is modest: the pipeline assembles existing components (Qwen LLM/MLLM, YOLOE, BLIP, ELLA-style semantic connector), and the metric design (MLLM yes/no checks per attribute) is a natural extension of T2I-CompBench/DPG-Bench-style VQA checking to longer prompts. The contribution is primarily resource-based and empirical rather than conceptual.

The nine-region spatial partitioning scheme (Appendix B) is somewhat ad hoc: the overlapping regions [0.3-0.7] leave a large uncharacterized zone, and 32.68% of characters still receive 'null' locations; the claim of 'optimal balance' is supported only by a comparison to the naive 3x3 grid rather than against alternatives (e.g., finer grids, quadrant schemes).

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence: e.g., attributing failure hierarchies to 'text encoders that fail to capture syntactic dependencies' is inferred from aggregate model-family comparisons rather than a controlled probe of encoder capability; and the benchmark's own acknowledged bias toward realistic styles limits the scope of the style-attribute findings.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a genuine gap: prior long-prompt T2I evaluations (DensePrompts, DPG-Bench) use far shorter prompts and coarse metrics, whereas DETAILMASTER averages 284.89 tokens with structured annotations across four dimensions (37,165 character attributes, 6,910 locations, 18,526 relationships), as summarized in Table 1.

The controlled 2x2 ablation (Table 3) is the most interesting part of the paper: it disentangles token-limit expansion from long-prompt training and shows that training data matters more than context window (77-limit w/ long-prompt training beats 512-limit w/ short-prompt training), supported by short-prompt transfer checks (Appendix U).

The evaluation of 19 models across five paradigms (Table 2) yields a useful difficulty hierarchy (Character Locations and Person Attributes hardest; Scene Attributes near-saturated), with error-source analysis (Appendix R) that gives actionable diagnoses such as conflicts between instructions and real-world positional priors.

Robustness efforts are above average for benchmark papers: cross-evaluator replication with InternVL3-9B with Kendall's tau ~0.88-1.0 (Appendix J), self-enhancement bias check for Qwen-Image (Table 11), randomness analysis (Appendix L), a lightweight 3B evaluator and 800-prompt mini-benchmark that preserve rankings (Appendices K, N), and human evaluation of annotation quality (Section 5.2, Appendix G).
Full release of data, pipeline, and code (implemented in Data-Juicer) plus a lightweight evaluator lowers adoption barriers.
weaknesses: The central validity concern is not fully resolved: the benchmark's ground truth and its judge are both produced by the same MLLM family (Qwen2.5-VL). While the authors show rankings are preserved under InternVL3-9B, they never validate that the MLLM's binary judgments on *generated* images agree with human judgments. Human evaluation (Appendix G) is performed only on the benchmark's annotations/source images, not on model outputs, so the accuracy of the evaluation workflow itself is unestablished. Given that fine-grained attributes (e.g., 'embossed design', 'crosscut at the top') require precisely the judgments 7B MLLMs are weakest at, this is a material gap.

The claim that prompts are 'grounded in real image-caption pairs to ensure visual realism and structural logic' is weaker than presented. The final prompts are LLM-augmented synthetic expansions (attributes added beyond the source image, verified against the final prompt rather than the image; Appendix I reports 60-93% attribute loss in original captions). The authors candidly state the prompt is the sole supervision, but then the pipeline's grounding value over purely LLM-generated prompts (which they criticize in Section 2) is diminished and the residual relationship annotation noise (88.58% Entity-Relationship-Image Alignment, Table 8) propagates into the benchmark.

The headline finding of a negative correlation between prompt length and adherence (Section 4.3) is confounded: longer prompts contain more attributes per character and more constraints per sample, so lower per-attribute accuracy is partly a mechanical effect of constraint density rather than 'length' per se. The paper conflates token count with constraint density without disentangling them (e.g., no fixed-constraint-count, varying-length analysis).

The ablation study trains only a Timestep-Aware Semantic Connector on a frozen SD-XL with 2M pairs (Appendix C.2); conclusions about 'long-prompt training matters more than token capacity' are drawn from this single narrow configuration and may not transfer to full fine-tuning or modern architectures.

Several insights are confirmatory rather than new: better encoders help, unified models scale well, SOTA proprietary models still plateau around 50% on relational tasks - these largely restate what DPG-Bench and others already suggested, now with denser prompts.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: duplicated HPSv2 references (2023a/2023b), typos ('Fliter', 'are tend to leak', 'an challenge'), and references to future-dated works (OneIG-Bench 'NeurIPS 38, 2026', Nano Banana 2 '2026', ICLR 2026 citations) that are not verifiable. Some conclusions lean on these unverifiable sources (Appendix Q).

Comparability concerns across the 19 models: resolutions differ (512 vs 1024), guidance scales and step counts vary by model, and the best available backbone is substituted for some long-prompt methods where paper configurations are unavailable (Appendix C.1), introducing confounds in cross-model comparisons that the paper does not analyze.

strengths: Substantial and well-motivated benchmark contribution: 4,116 expert-validated prompts averaging ~285 tokens, far longer than prior long-prompt benchmarks (DensePrompts ~100, DPG-Bench ~84 tokens), with rich structured annotations across four compositional dimensions (Table 1).

Careful, multi-stage data construction pipeline grounded in real image–caption pairs (DOCCI, Localized Narratives) with auxiliary grounding tools (YOLOE open-set detection, BLIP re-ranking, MLLM verification), which partially mitigates the hallucination risks of pure LLM synthesis.
Extensive evaluation breadth: 19 models across five paradigms, including proprietary SOTA systems and the newly released Nano Banana 2, providing a useful snapshot of the field.

Highly informative ablation (Table 3) that cleanly disentangles token-limit expansion from long-prompt training, supporting the paper's most interesting claim: that long-prompt training matters more than context window size, and that the two are synergistic. The T2I-CompBench cross-check (Appendix U) adds value.

Unusually thorough robustness treatment for a benchmark paper: cross-evaluator re-ranking with InternVL3-9B (Kendall's Tau 0.88–1.0), lightweight-evaluator validation, randomness analysis, and direct testing of the self-enhancement bias concern for family-matched Qwen encoder/evaluator pairs (Table 11).
Human evaluation of 400 samples with multi-component checks per annotation type, plus a quantitative analysis of attribute loss in original captions (Table 9) that motivates the pipeline.
Promises open-source data, code, and a mini-benchmark with a resource-light evaluator, which supports reproducibility and adoption.
weaknesses: The central measurement instrument — Qwen2.5-VL-7B judging fine-grained attribute presence, positions, and relationships in generated images — is never validated against human judgment on generated images. Human evaluation is applied to the dataset annotations, not to the evaluator's verdicts on model outputs; the cross-MLLM consistency checks (Appendix J) show evaluator–evaluator agreement, which does not establish correctness. Given absolute accuracies drive all conclusions (e.g., the ~50% plateau for SOTA models), this is a material gap.

The paper criticizes prior benchmarks for LLM-generated prompts that 'risk violating real-world physical logic,' yet its own prompts are LLM-expanded with details deliberately not present in the source image. The authors argue this is fine because evaluation matches final prompts rather than source images (Appendix G), which is internally consistent but means DETAILMASTER measures adherence to synthetic, potentially unnatural instructions — a different construct than 'professional-grade prompt adherence' as claimed.

Some entity-relationship and scene annotations exhibit notable misalignment with source images (88.58% and 91% per Tables 7–8), and the residual noise propagates into constraint lists even if prompts are internally consistent.

Key mechanistic claims — e.g., that CLIP-based failures indicate encoders 'struggle to preserve syntactic dependencies,' and the 'attribute leakage' explanation — are plausible but inferential; error-pattern analyses (Appendix R) are qualitative rather than a controlled causal test.

The ablation study's external validity is limited: conclusions are drawn from a single architecture (SD-XL with a frozen UNet, only the Timestep-Aware Semantic Connector trained) on ~2M pairs; the 'long-prompt training matters more' claim may not generalize to from-scratch or fully fine-tuned training regimes.

Model comparisons in Table 2 conflate scale, data, and architecture; the attributed drivers of unified-model success (MoT, UniCap, scale) are asserted from prior papers' self-descriptions rather than tested.

Statistical rigor is thin: no confidence intervals, no per-sample variance estimates for the main table, and the human evaluation uses only 2 annotators on 400 samples without inter-annotator agreement.

Presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('Fliter', 'attributes are tend to leak'), occasional duplicated references (Wu et al. 2023a/b), and heavy reliance on appendices for core detail (evaluation pipeline, ablation setup).
